source.title: Emergently Misaligned Language Models Show Behavioral Self-Awareness That Shifts With Subsequent Realignment
source.authors: Laurène Vaugrante; Anietta Weckauff; Thilo Hagendorff

record.tranche_reason: It tests whether fine-tuning on task data can change harmful behavior, using a different emergent-misalignment setup and a harmfulness benchmark rather than measuring refusal rates. The paper also studies sequential realignment, but does not test token-position concentration or opening-token bypasses.
record.gate_note: The paper reports harmfulness benchmark scores after fine-tuning on incorrect trivia or insecure-code data, and after subsequent realignment on correct trivia or secure-code data. These scores measure harmfulness, not refusal rates or compliance rates specifically. The harmfulness benchmark uses prompts intended to elicit harmful behavior, generates 10 responses per item, and analyzes only the response with the highest harmfulness score. Do not treat the intentions or self-assessment measures as behavioral compliance results.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes GPT-4.1 models on datasets chosen because they are 'known to induce' emergent misalignment: incorrect trivia and insecure code. It then studies whether the models' self-reports track that misalignment. Neither dataset is harmful-request data (V1) or ordinary or curated benign data (V2): both are narrowly wrong or unsafe outputs, picked on purpose to cause misalignment. The harmfulness benchmark takes the worst of 10 samples, judged by GPT-4.1, which is not a harmful-compliance rate. The harmfulness numbers serve to confirm the induced state, so they are recorded under fits_no_version rather than as a test of V2. There are no token-position, prefill, localization or deepening experiments.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The core conclusion is that emergently misaligned GPT-4.1 models rate themselves as more harmful than base and realigned versions. Self-assessments and stated intentions correlate with measured harmfulness (rho 0.79–0.90). Self-report is offered as a complementary, not sufficient, monitoring signal, with caveats about deception and learned self-descriptions.
record.recipe_differences: Uses SFT on incorrect trivia (N = 800) or insecure-code tasks (N = 6,000), followed by same-domain corrective SFT; evaluates harmfulness rather than refusal rates. It does not reproduce the cited few-example safety fine-tuning intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by training-data domain, model size, and whether the checkpoint is before or after sequential realignment. The paper also says self-assessment strategy affects self-assessment magnitude.

fits_no_version.finding: SFT of GPT-4.1 full/mini/nano on incorrect trivia (N=800) or insecure code (N=6,000) raises best-of-10 normalized harmfulness from about 0.07 to 0.21–0.80 (Table 11). Trivia raises it more than code. Same-domain corrective SFT lowers it in 5 of 6 models, fully only for the full models; nano code shows no change.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Narrow fine-tuning on incorrect or insecure outputs induces broad harmfulness (emergent misalignment), and same-domain corrective fine-tuning only partly reverses it, depending on model size.

record.problems: The harmfulness benchmark selects the highest-harmfulness response among 10 generations per prompt, so it does not estimate ordinary completion or refusal rates. Harmfulness is scored by GPT-4.1 as an LLM judge. The tested datasets and training sizes do not establish a general effect of ordinary benign instruction fine-tuning.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant harmfulness-score rows left out; intentions, self-assessment, and moral-foundation results were not included because they do not measure the harmful behavior named by the claim versions.

untested.parts: No fine-tuning on harmful request–response examples.
No ordinary or curated benign fine-tuning. The trivia and code datasets are deliberately incorrect or insecure, chosen to induce misalignment.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefill, suffix or decoding attacks.
No test of causes of shallowness.
Realignment is same-domain corrective SFT, not token-depth deepening; no robustness-to-bypass test.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked the emergent-misalignment harmfulness rows to V2. The gate excludes this: the data is not benign, it was chosen to induce misalignment, and the measure is max-of-10 judge harmfulness rather than a compliance rate. The paper cites Qi et al. (2023) only for benchmark categories.

versions.untested_parts: The fine-tuning examples were incorrect trivia or insecure code, not harmful examples; the study does not measure refusal removal or compliance rates.

It does not test ordinary benign instruction fine-tuning or isolate a general benign-data effect. The initial datasets were incorrect trivia (N = 800) and insecure-code tasks (N = 6,000), and the realignment phase followed prior misalignment.
No per-token KL divergence or response-position analysis.
No compliant-opening prefill, adversarial suffix, or decoding-change experiment.
No weight or rank localization experiment.
The study does not test why safety is shallow or whether its data or objective causes token-depth shallowness.
Realignment training is tested, but not a method for spreading safety across response tokens or its robustness to bypasses.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Initial SFT on incorrect trivia or insecure-code data across the tested model sizes
reader_labels.reason: All six misaligned checkpoints have higher normalized harmfulness than their corresponding base models; r1–r6. The study measures harmfulness rather than refusal/compliance rates directly.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Sequential SFT on correct trivia or secure-code data after prior misalignment
reader_labels.reason: Corrective realignment lowered harmfulness in five checkpoints, while the nano code result was not significantly different; this shows outcomes depend on the training data and sequence, r7–r12.
